name: !!actor-title
text: INZBC AI Operating System

name: !!actor-body
text:
A governed intelligence platform for the India New Zealand Business Council
Bhanu Gupta · Roshan Aryal · Paras
Studio 5, Block 3 2026 — Final Presentation
textPreview: | A governed intelligence platform for the India New Zealand Business Council | Bhanu Gupta · Roshan Aryal · Paras | Studio 5, Block 3 20...

text: We’re Bhanu Gupta, Roshan Aryal and Paras. Over ten weeks, we worked with Sunil Kaushal and the India New Zealand Business Council to turn a recurring operational problem into a governed software platform. Today we’ll show the problem, the controls, what failed during development, and the working system.

name: !!actor-kicker
text: THE PROBLEM

name: !!actor-title
text: Staff do the same work every morning
textPreview: Staff do the same work every morning

name: !!actor-body
text:
INZBC is volunteer-run. A handful of people read the same news sources, answer the same FTA tariff questions, and draft the same member communications by hand.

The quality of what reaches members depends on who did it that day.

The council did not ask for an AI that writes things.
They asked for software that takes the repetitive middle of the work — and never puts an unchecked claim in front of a member.
textPreview: INZBC is volunteer-run. A handful of people read the same news sources, answer the same FTA tariff questions, and draft the same member c...

text: INZBC is volunteer-run, so valuable staff time disappears into repetitive daily work: scanning sources, answering tariff questions, and drafting member updates. The risk is inconsistency. The brief was therefore not ‘let AI write’; it was to automate the middle while refusing any unchecked claim at the member boundary.

name: !!actor-kicker
text: WHAT WE BUILT

name: !!actor-title
text: One application, four modules

name: !!actor-body
text:
Strategic Intelligence Platform — turns public news into an approved daily brief
FTA Explainer — answers tariff questions from a sourced corpus, with citations
Communications Assistant — drafts member content for a named human approver
Member Portal — member-facing shell; membership stays in Member Jungle

One FastAPI backend. One PostgreSQL database. One React application.

We built one application with four connected modules. SIP creates an approved intelligence brief; the FTA Explainer answers from a cited corpus; the Communications Assistant drafts only for named human approval; and the Member Portal is the member-facing shell. They share one backend, database, and React interface.

name: !!actor-kicker
text: THE DESIGN IDEA

name: !!actor-title
text: The system refuses rather than guesses
textPreview: The system refuses rather than guesses

name: !!actor-body
text:
A brief cannot be distributed unless a named reviewer approved it, the CEO ruled Continue, and no critical QA failure is open.
The analyst who wrote a brief cannot record its QA result — checked against recorded acts, not job titles, so it holds when one person wears several hats.
The audit log cannot be edited. Fifteen triggers refuse UPDATE and DELETE; the application role is granted INSERT and SELECT only.
Distribution is off by default. So is CORS. A missing redaction policy refuses the call.

One file in ~10,000 lines calls a model provider. The FTA Explainer calls none.
textPreview: A brief cannot be distributed unless a named reviewer approved it, the CEO ruled Continue, and no critical QA failure is open. | The anal...

text: The central design choice was refusal. Workflow state, recorded actions, database constraints, audit triggers, and deployment switches are intended to block unsafe paths before output reaches a member. That includes separation of duties, critical QA gates, redaction rules, and production distribution being disabled by default.

name: !!actor-kicker
text: HOW IT WORKS

name: !!actor-title
text: SIP architecture

This is the Strategic Intelligence Platform flow. Public sources are collected and normalized, candidates are scored and reviewed, a brief is drafted, QA is recorded, and only then can a CEO decision and distribution occur. Each step writes state and evidence back to the governed backend.

name: !!actor-kicker
text: HOW IT WORKS

name: !!actor-title
text: FTA Explainer: no model in the path
textPreview: FTA Explainer: no model in the path

name: !!actor-body
text:
You asked at the mid-point how the system generates answers and whether they can be trusted.
For the FTA Explainer, nothing is generated. Every answer comes from a corpus entry carrying a chapter-and-article citation. No match escalates to a person — it does not approximate.
textPreview: You asked at the mid-point how the system generates answers and whether they can be trusted. | For the FTA Explainer, nothing is generate...

text: The FTA Explainer deliberately keeps a language model out of the answer path. A user’s tariff question is matched against a curated corpus, and the response carries the relevant chapter and article citation. If the system cannot resolve a match, it escalates to a person instead of inventing an answer.

name: !!actor-kicker
text: HOW IT WORKS

name: !!actor-title
text: Comms Assistant: the boundary comes first
textPreview: Comms Assistant: the boundary comes first

name: !!actor-body
text: Member records, CRM notes, board papers and private messages are refused before a prompt is built — not filtered out of the answer afterwards.
textPreview: Member records, CRM notes, board papers and private messages are refused before a prompt is built — not filtered out of the answer afterw...

text: For communications, the boundary is enforced before prompting. Member records, CRM notes, board papers, and private messages are rejected before a prompt is assembled. The model can help draft public-source material, but it never receives content that the policy classifies as private or restricted.

name: !!actor-kicker
text: A DECISION, AND ITS PAYOFF

name: !!actor-title
text: Why PostgreSQL, and why it mattered
textPreview: Why PostgreSQL, and why it mattered

name: !!actor-body
text:
We compared PostgreSQL against MongoDB. The argument for a document store is schema flexibility. The argument against, here, is that our hardest requirements are constraint-shaped.

A run must not sit in a state its decisions do not justify. A report version must not be submitted before it was created. One line of SQL each — application code everywhere else.

The payoff, months later: an end-to-end test started failing intermittently. The CHECK constraint submitted_at >= created_at was refusing rows. The constraint was right — the host clock and the database container clock were 0.44 seconds apart, so records really were dated after they were stored.

We chose the database that could refuse. It refused something real.
textPreview: We compared PostgreSQL against MongoDB. The argument for a document store is schema flexibility. The argument against, here, is that our ...

text: We chose PostgreSQL because our requirements were constraint-shaped: legal workflow transitions, time ordering, audit immutability, and role-limited writes. That choice paid off when the database exposed a real clock mismatch between application and host. The refusal was inconvenient, but it proved the control was active.

name: !!actor-kicker
text: HONESTY

name: !!actor-title
text: What we got wrong

name: !!actor-body
text:
Four controls existed, were tested, and were never reachable. Specification said the rule existed; a test asserted it; the enforcing code was never called. We had built reassurance.
→ Now a conformance test refuses to merge any route with no declared authority.

A content hash covered an empty digest regardless of what the analyst selected — and still produced a valid-looking hash. Silent, and the hash is the whole record of what was submitted.

One test flake, two wrong diagnoses. Rate-limiter state, then database pollution. Both fitted the symptoms. Neither was the cause.

Every one of these was quiet. That is the lesson we are taking out of Studio 5.
textPreview: Four controls existed, were tested, and were never reachable. Specification said the rule existed; a test asserted it; the enforcing code...

text: The most useful lessons came from quiet failures. Some controls existed in code and tests but were not reachable from routes; a content hash looked valid while covering the wrong material; and a flaky test attracted two plausible but incorrect diagnoses. Our response was to add stronger conformance checks and trace enforcement end to end.

name: !!actor-kicker
text: OUTCOME

name: !!actor-title
text: Where it stands

name: !!actor-body
text:
Released as v1.0.0. Five of six objectives achieved.
The sixth — production deployment — was deliberately not attempted. It is INZBC's decision and it has not been made. production_enabled is false.

What is ready: one command brings the system up on a clean machine; versioned migrations that refuse to run against a database they do not match; operator, incident and recovery guides.
What is not: the system has been tested, not used. No brief has been produced on a Tuesday morning when someone needed it.

Version one is released, with five of six objectives achieved. Production deployment remains intentionally unattempted because that decision belongs to INZBC, and production remains disabled. The system is reproducible and documented, but our honest limitation is that it has been tested extensively rather than used through a real working week.

name: !!actor-kicker
text: RECOMMENDATIONS

name: !!actor-title
text: What we would do next

name: !!actor-body
text:
1. Close the four open decisions with INZBC. Everything about deployment waits on them.
2. Run one real brief end to end with staff, in a working week, before enabling anything.
3. Add a second reviewer account. The separation-of-duties control already supports it — no code change needed.
4. Commission an independent accessibility audit before the public site goes live.
5. Keep writing the decision records. They are cheap to maintain and expensive to reconstruct.
textPreview: 1. Close the four open decisions with INZBC. Everything about deployment waits on them. | 2. Run one real brief end to end with staff, in...

text: Our next steps are deliberately practical: close the four client decisions, run one genuine brief with staff, add a second reviewer account, commission an accessibility audit before public launch, and keep the decision records current. The first real operating week should happen before any production switch is enabled.

name: !!actor-kicker
text: LIVE

name: !!actor-title
text: Demonstration

name: !!actor-body
text:
1. Choose a run under Runs & Candidates — ten runs, real states from the database
2. Brief Builder loads that run's own candidates and its recorded source coverage
3. CEO Decision: "Not reachable yet — this run is currently Report Drafted. The CEO decision opens once QA has passed."

That refusal is the state machine enforcing itself against the database.
It is the whole argument of the project in one screen.
textPreview: 1. Choose a run under Runs & Candidates — ten runs, real states from the database | 2. Brief Builder loads that run's own candidates and ...

text: In the live demonstration, watch the backend state rather than the interface polish. We select a real run, load only that run’s candidates and coverage, then attempt a CEO decision too early. The system refuses because QA has not passed. That refusal is the project’s core claim made visible.
